About this citation

The 'Western Inscription' (Ximing 西銘) is a separate short text by Zhang Zai that was later incorporated into the Zhengmeng as its first chapter; the two names are not interchangeable in Chinese scholarship.

### Reading the cited source

The archive attributes this English wording to Zhengmeng, Western Inscription (Wing-tsit Chan translation) and files it under Neo-Confucianism.

[What a locator tells you, and what it does not](https://www.philosophydef.com/sourcing-method#locators) · [How this archive traces a quotation](https://www.philosophydef.com/quote-source)

#### About Zhang Zai

Zhang Zai (1020–1077) was a Northern Song Neo-Confucian cosmologist and moral thinker associated with the “gas” (qi) metaphysics of the period. Teaching in Guanzhong, he influenced later Cheng-Zhu orthodoxy even where they revised him.

### Interpretation

The Western Inscription opens Zhang Zai's account of what a person is: made of the same qi as everything else, small but not separate. From this cosmology the ethics follows in the next lines — all people are my siblings, all things my companions, so care for them is not charity toward strangers but conduct within one body. The passage became the canonical statement of Neo-Confucian unity with all things, and the "four sentences" (establish the mind for Heaven and Earth…) extend it from belonging into vocation.

#### Why it matters

It grounds concern for strangers and the natural world in shared constitution rather than sentiment — on this view you do not decide to include them, they were never excluded. Read as an actual claim about matter rather than a metaphor, it makes environmental ethics an internal affair.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “Heaven is my father and Earth is my…”?

“Heaven is my father and Earth is my…” comes from Zhengmeng, Western Inscription (Wing-tsit Chan translation) (11th century CE), attributed to Zhang Zai.

#### What does Zhang Zai mean by nature?

Nature may mean physical cosmos, living world, human nature, or a normative standard of what ought to be. Presocratics, Daoists, Stoics, and modern environmental thinkers share the word while disagreeing about its force. This passage enters that discussion through nature, humanity.
